Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

issues.item: Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible
issues.explanation: For trauma involving a child's life-threatening illness, revenge-focused ideation about identifiable responsible people is hard to reconcile unless there was clear culpability (e.g. negligence), which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in the profile. It appears clinically mismatched to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: Generalized threat from strangers and scanning faces for danger fit interpersonal assault or public violence better than a child's medical crisis. These threat items imply fear of hostile people in ordinary situations, but the rest of the profile does not provide a coherent bridge from the illness trauma to stranger-based danger expectations.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Intense rage on recall could occur, but here it primarily supports the revenge item and interpersonal-threat theme. In combination with the stranger-threat items, it pulls the profile toward an assault/perpetrator formulation rather than a child's illness trauma formulation.

issues.item: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
issues.explanation: Meaning seeking is not inherently maladaptive and, in this profile, sits awkwardly with the otherwise threat-trigger-memory driven formulation; it does not clearly function as an avoidance/safety strategy tied to the selected triggers, threat items, or memory pattern.

issues.item: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
issues.explanation: Hypervigilance for interpersonal threat in faces/body language is difficult to reconcile with the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, where danger is more plausibly linked to medical cues, loss cues, or signs of illness rather than hostile people.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Needing to stay alert to fall asleep implies ongoing external danger monitoring; for a trauma centered on a child's illness, this would usually require clearer linkage to caregiving/medical monitoring, which is absent from the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
issues.explanation: For the indexed trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, 'anything that reminds me of someone I have lost' implies bereavement/loss rather than ongoing threat or illness trauma. That is a hard-to-explain mismatch unless the child died, which is not the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
issues.explanation: Within the overall profile, the dominant theme is fear/hypervigilance/disorientation around threat cues (sirens, crying, startle, sleep vigilance, physical reactivity, confused/unreal memory). 'Intense rage' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the rest of the profile and sits awkwardly beside suppression of anger, making this item clinically less coherent than the others.

vignette: Mateo had been fifteen when his younger brother, Tomás, suddenly collapsed during a weekend soccer match. One moment they were running side by side; the next, Tomás was on the concrete, convulsing, his lips turning a pale, ashen gray. Mateo remembered pressing his hands against his brother's chest, trying to will air into lungs that no longer responded. The world narrowed to the frantic rhythm of his own heartbeat and the thick, coppery scent of panic that clung to his own skin. Emergency responders arrived within minutes. The wail of their sirens cut through the afternoon heat, growing louder with every passing second. In the back of the ambulance, Tomás was intubated, his body slick with cold sweat, his breaths reduced to shallow, desperate sobs. The hospital corridors were a blur of urgent commands, flashing monitors, and a nurse's sudden, quiet weeping in a supply room. Tomás survived, but only after days hovering between life and death, suspended in a sterile, fluorescent-lit limbo. In the months that followed, Mateo's nervous system never returned to its baseline. Ordinary sounds now hijacked his attention. A car backfiring on his commute made him jolt against the steering wheel, his shoulders hiking to his ears. He was certain that if he let his guard down for even a second, another emergency would catch him unprepared. At night, he lay awake with his eyes fixed on the ceiling, refusing to drift into sleep. He needed to stay alert, to monitor the quiet of his apartment for any sign that something was wrong. When the memories of that afternoon surfaced, they did not arrive in a clear line. They crashed into him in fragments: a nurse's hand, the smell of antiseptic, a sudden gasp from the monitors, the way Tomás's fingers had curled inward. He could not place them in order. The narrative felt too extreme, too catastrophic to be real, yet the terror it summoned was identical to what he had felt on the asphalt. The physical reaction was immediate-a tightening in his throat, a rapid pulse, a cold sweat breaking across his palms. He experienced these symptoms side by side, each occupying the same breathless space. As a data scientist, Mateo spent his days building predictive models in an open-plan office where the ambient hum of servers was constant. Avoidance of medical cues had become a quiet, daily discipline. He declined workplace health screenings, scheduled his own annual physicals for holidays when he could go early, and changed his route past the urgent care clinic on 4th Street to avoid the flashing lights. The olfactory trigger arrived unbidden one Tuesday during a quarterly review. A colleague had just returned from the gym, the sharp, saline tang of fresh sweat cutting through the office's recycled air. Mateo felt his chest clamp shut. He stood abruptly, knocking his chair back, and walked to the stairwell without explanation. He told himself he just needed air, though what he needed was to escape the sudden certainty that the room was filling with the same damp, frantic odor he had smelled in that ambulance. When a child cried in the grocery store, his hands went numb. When he felt frustration rise, he never allowed himself to feel or express anger. He simply turned his attention elsewhere, trying hard not to think about the trauma. Over weeks, these habits solidified. He stopped answering after-hours calls, began wearing long sleeves in summer, and stopped inviting friends over, telling them his schedule was unpredictable. By the time he walked into the clinic, Mateo was exhausted from the effort of staying constantly vigilant. He had come to believe that his brother's survival had been a fluke, something that could happen to anyone at any moment. The final push to seek help came when he realized he could no longer focus on his code. The numbers no longer aligned in his mind; the patterns blurred into the chaotic fragments of a boy who had almost died. He wanted to sleep through the night without his eyes darting toward the door. He hoped someone could help him untangle the memories so they would stop carrying the same weight. What frightened him most was not the past itself, but the feeling that the ground beneath him was still giving way, and he was running out of ways to hold it together.
